name: Biochanin A
lead: Biochanin A is an O-methylated isoflavone, a plant phytoestrogen found in red clover, soy, alfalfa sprouts, peanuts and chickpea.[1] In hair-care marketing it appears as a red clover-derived component of Capixyl, a cosmetic active that combines a peptide with isoflavones and is positioned as a topical aid for hair density and the look of thinning hair.[2]

People encounter biochanin A in two ways: through topical hair products that list red clover isoflavones, and through red clover extracts sold as supplements, including ones that appear in the "support" stacks discussed on bodybuilding forums.[11][12] Its estrogen-receptor activity in laboratory assays is the basis on which it is associated with hair-care use.[3]

No clinical study of biochanin A for hair has been published. Research on red clover isoflavones concerns other areas, such as menopausal symptoms, bone, bladder function and blood glucose, and a 2025 review lists Capixyl among topical hair actives.[2][6][13][16][17]
infobox: Red clover, soy, alfalfa sprouts, peanut, chickpea[1]

paras: Biochanin A is an O-methylated isoflavone with the formula C16H12O5. Its systematic name is 5,7-dihydroxy-4'-methoxyisoflavone, and it is also called 4'-methylgenistein or genistein 4-methyl ether, which describes its relationship to the soy isoflavone genistein.[1] It occurs in red clover (Trifolium pratense), soy, alfalfa sprouts, peanuts, chickpea and other legumes.[1]

Reviews of phytoestrogens list biochanin A alongside daidzein, genistein and formononetin as one of the best-known isoflavone phytoestrogens, with soy and clover products as main dietary sources.[9][10] Plant enzymes such as biochanin-A reductase and a malonyltransferase act on it and its glucoside, which are described in the biochemical literature on the compound.[1]

In hair care, biochanin A is named as one of the isoflavone components of red clover extract used in the cosmetic active Capixyl, which is added to topical serums and lotions marketed for hair density.[2] A 2025 review of topical alternatives for hair loss lists Capixyl among the non-drug actives in use.[2]
Red clover extract is also sold as an oral supplement, and appears in multi-ingredient stacks that forum users describe as supporting hormone balance during training cycles.[11][12]

Biochanin A is classed as a phytoestrogen: isoflavones are among the most estrogenic plant compounds and can have estrogen-like or anti-estrogenic effects depending on context.[9] A 1998 binding study examined how phytoestrogens interact with estrogen receptor subtypes, including ER beta.[3] Wikipedia also describes it as a weak inhibitor of fatty acid amide hydrolase in vitro and as a ligand of the aryl hydrocarbon receptor.[1] Natural-product screening reviews have examined isoflavones as PPAR gamma ligands.[14]
No mechanism specific to hair growth has been established for biochanin A.

Human bioavailability has been characterised for isoflavones such as genistein and daidzein and their glycosides in healthy women, showing efficient intestinal absorption with differences between glycoside and non-glycoside forms.[4] Comparable data for biochanin A are less prominent.
No studies found on biochanin A for hair. Studies of red clover isoflavones address other conditions.

subs.h: Related research on red clover isoflavones
paras: A 2021 meta-analysis of eight randomized trials found red clover extract associated with about 1.7 fewer hot flushes per day than placebo in peri- and postmenopausal women, with larger differences reported in groups with at least five hot flushes a day, longer follow-up, higher isoflavone doses and formulations richer in biochanin A.[6] An earlier Cochrane review assessed phytoestrogens for hot flushes and night sweats.[15]

Other randomized trials have examined red clover extract for blood glucose, overactive bladder symptoms, vaginal and sexual health, mammographic breast density and endometrial effects in postmenopausal women.[16][17][18][19][20] Registered trials cover osteopenia, urge incontinence and menopausal symptoms with lipid profile.[7][8][13]

Reviews describe isoflavones as potentially beneficial in hormone-related conditions and also as possible endocrine disruptors in parts of the population, so their hormonal activity is discussed in both directions.[9] A systematic review of dietary isoflavones and female hormone-dependent cancers examined benefit and risk.[22] No safety data for topical use of biochanin A on the scalp were found.

lore.intro: Red clover extract is mentioned on T Nation in connection with phytoestrogen and estrogen-management supplement stacks rather than hair.[11][12][23]

claims.claim: Red clover is a useful ingredient in hormone-support stacks
claims.believers: Users list red clover extract among ingredients in commercial support products and in their own stacks alongside saw palmetto and similar extracts.[11][12]
claims.experts: Red clover isoflavone extracts have been studied mainly for menopausal symptoms, where a meta-analysis reported modest reductions in hot flushes.[6] No studies have tested it in these stack contexts.

claims.claim: Phytoestrogens can block receptor binding of stronger estrogens
claims.believers: A forum poster quotes coach Charles Poliquin's site as saying plant phytoestrogens can inhibit receptor binding of human and chemical estrogens.[23]
claims.experts: Isoflavones bind estrogen receptors in laboratory assays and can act as weak estrogens or anti-estrogens depending on context.[3][9]

claims.claim: Biochanin A in Capixyl supports hair density
claims.believers: Product marketing names red clover isoflavones as a component of the active.[2]
claims.experts: No clinical study of biochanin A for hair has been published.[2]

card.summary: Red-clover isoflavone named in Capixyl; studied for other things, not hair.

quick.overview:
Biochanin A is a phytoestrogen from red clover and legumes. Hair-care marketing lists it as a component of Capixyl.
No hair-specific human study was found; trials of red clover isoflavones address menopause and bone.
quick.mechanism: It binds estrogen receptors in laboratory assays and weakly inhibits an enzyme in vitro; no hair-growth mechanism is established.
quick.risks: As a phytoestrogen it has hormone-receptor activity in lab work; no safety data for topical hair use were found.

chain: Red clover isoflavone included in topical hair-care formulas
Phytoestrogen activity at estrogen receptors in laboratory assays
angle.text: Biochanin A is used in appearance terms as an ingredient in cosmetic hair products such as Capixyl, where it is marketed as a plant-derived active for the look of fuller hair. People also take red clover extract orally, and some discuss it as a phytoestrogen within supplement stacks.
